svg.title: One-way extranet and shared services: making reachability deliberately asymmetric without new hardware
svg.desc: Left panel shows a one-way extranet between a customer VRF and a partner VRF. The customer exports a shared-services route target and the partner imports only that target, so the partner can reach the named prefixes while the customer learns nothing from the partner. An arrow marks the direction of the import, which is the whole mechanism. Right panel shows a shared-services VRF serving several customer VRFs: each customer imports the services target, and the services VRF imports every customer target so it can reply. A note explains that the return path is what makes services work, and that it must be limited to the services prefixes. A bottom band lists the three checks for any extranet design: who initiates, which direction needs a return path, and what stops the partner from reaching anything else.
svg.text: Extranet is RT direction, not a new device and not a new cable
The import list is the firewall rule; the export list is what you offer
The partner reaches the shared prefixes and nothing else.
The customer learns nothing from the partner in return.
One import line, and the business relationship is encoded.
Each customer imports the services target; the services
VRF imports every customer target, so it can reply.
The catch: a server replies to whoever connects, so the services VRF needs the return path. Limit what it imports to the customer prefixes it serves, and
remember that this makes the services VRF a possible transit point between customers if its import list is ever widened “to fix a quick problem”.

text.tspan: Three questions before any extranet change:

svg.text: 1. Who initiates the session? The initiator needs a route out, the responder needs a route back — one import line each, not one shared line.
2. Which prefixes exactly? Importing a whole VRF “because it is easier” is how a partner gains a path to every branch you own.
3. What stops them going further? The RT only controls entry; routing and ACLs inside the VRF must control onward reachability.
